The mouth's three main jobs are chewing, swallowing and speaking; breathing and showing emotion are secondary. Chewing Chewing is a steady rhythm of opening and closing, and it's the first step of digestion. Sensors in the gums and ligaments around the teeth, the tongue, the joints and the muscles report to the brainstem, which fires some muscles and quiets others. A "pattern generator" in the brainstem stores learned patterns (engrams), so chewing runs mostly on autopilot, like walking. If you bite something hard by surprise, a reflex stops the closing muscles and opens the jaw at once. Each stroke opens mostly straight down, swings to the side at the bottom, then closes at an angle to crush the food and finishes with a small sideways grinding slide. A chewing stroke opens only about 16-18 mm and moves about 5-6 mm sideways. On the food side the jaw opens forward and comes back as it closes. Early in a bite there is more forward and sideways movement; it gets smaller as the food breaks down. Harder food means more sideways movement. About 78% of people chew mostly on one side, usually the side with the best contacts. Teeth do touch while chewing, more often as the food gets softer, almost every stroke before swallowing, for about 0.2 seconds each, and they always come back to MIP ("home plate"). Tall cusps make an up-and-down stroke; flat or worn cusps make a wider one. Someone who grinds flat has no single MIP, just a zone. People with jaw pain chew slower, shorter and less evenly. Bite force: the strongest ever measured was 975 lb; men are about 118-142 lb, women about 79-99 lb. Back molars bite three to five times harder than front teeth, which is why front teeth can handle angled forces. Long-faced people bite softer; square-faced people bite harder. A filling left half a millimeter high doubles the force on that tooth. Most serious chewing happens at the second premolar and first molar. Dentures give only a fraction of normal force. The tongue is the mouth's knife, fork and spoon, and the cheek muscle (buccinator) works with it. Swallowing Swallowing (deglutition) moves food from the mouth to the stomach, mostly by reflex. You decide to swallow based on how fine the food is, how much taste you've gotten out of it, and how wet it is. Adults steady the jaw by putting the teeth together in MIP (a somatic swallow). Babies, without teeth, push the tongue forward between the gums (a visceral swallow). Keeping that baby swallow too long pushes the front teeth forward and can cause an open bite. A swallow presses the teeth harder (about 66 lb) and longer than chewing. We swallow about 590 times a day. There are three stages. First, the tongue presses the food against the roof of the mouth with the lips closed and teeth together, and pushes it back. Second, throat muscles squeeze it down, the soft palate closes off the nose, the epiglottis covers the windpipe, and the ear tubes open; the first two stages take about a second. Third, the esophagus carries it to the stomach in about 6-7 seconds. Speech Air from the lungs passes the vocal cords, which make the pitch; the tongue, lips, cheeks and jaw shape the sound. Speech is a learned reflex, and the teeth do not touch while talking. For "f" and "v," the upper front teeth should just touch the line where the wet and dry parts of the lower lip meet; if they press into the lip they're too long, and if the sound is hard to make they may be too short. For "s," the teeth come closest (about 1-2 mm), which dentists use to judge bite height. For "m," the lips close and air goes out the nose.
